name: Barcelona
tagline: Gaudi's seaside capital of Catalan art and appetite.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Sep, Oct and Nov
whenBlurb: Come late May to June or in September for warm seas and lighter crowds; skip the hot, packed July-August peak and time it to a festival like La Merce.

ourTake.lede: Barcelona is Gaudí plus a great eating city, and both suffer from crowds, buy timed Sagrada Família tickets weeks ahead and go first thing for the morning light through the east windows. Park Güell is best at opening or last entry. Skip the Ramblas restaurants entirely; the real food is in a Gràcia or Sant Antoni bar most tourists never reach.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Gaudi, a beach in the city and long, late Mediterranean dinners.
ourTake.skipIf: You dislike crowds and are wary of pickpockets in busy quarters.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Barcelona
items.description: The city's finest address, a former bank on Passeig de Gràcia, all light, calm and quiet precision.

items.name: Hotel Arts Barcelona, A Ritz-Carlton Hotel
items.description: The great seafront tower, 44 storeys above the beach, under Gehry's golden fish.

items.name: Monument Hotel
items.description: A neo-Gothic Passeig de Gràcia mansion turned destination hotel, home to the city's first three-star table.

items.name: El Palace Barcelona
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's original grande dame, opened in 1919 as the Ritz, and still Barcelona's most classical grand hotel.

items.name: The Barcelona EDITION
items.description: Ian Schrager's cool, low-lit house in the old town, a rooftop and a nightclub under one modern roof.

items.name: The Cotton House Hotel, Autograph Collection
items.description: The former Cotton Textile Foundation, reborn, a spiral staircase, a library bar and old-world tailoring throughout.

items.name: Hotel Casa Fuster
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A 1911 Modernista landmark by Domènech i Montaner, the most beautiful building any Barcelona hotel occupies.

items.name: Majestic Hotel & Spa Barcelona
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A family-owned classic on Passeig de Gràcia, one block from Gaudí's La Pedrera.

items.name: Cotton House, annexe suites
items.description: The larger suites of the Cotton House, for a family taking more room in one of the Eixample's most characterful houses.

items.name: Mercer Hotel Barcelona
items.description: A boutique house built over a Roman wall in the Gothic Quarter, history you can touch, calm you can keep.

items.name: The Serras Barcelona
items.description: An intimate waterfront boutique on the site of Picasso's first studio, looking to the marina.

items.name: Almanac Barcelona
items.description: A sleek contemporary house on Gran Via with a rooftop pool and terrace over the city.

items.name: Ohla Eixample
items.description: A design-forward house wrapped in a rippling white façade, with a rooftop pool above the Eixample.

items.name: The One Barcelona, a Luxury Hotel
items.description: A quietly opulent H10 flagship a street from Passeig de Gràcia, with a rooftop plunge pool.

items.name: Alma Barcelona
items.description: A serene townhouse hotel around a hidden garden courtyard, a pocket of quiet off Passeig de Gràcia.

items.name: Wittmore Hotel
items.description: An adults-only townhouse tucked into a Gothic-Quarter lane, clubby, discreet and green-corniced.

items.name: Seventy Barcelona
items.description: A contemporary boutique in leafy Gràcia, away from the crowds, close to the neighbourhood's tables.

items.name: Soho House Barcelona
items.description: The members' club's seafront house in the old town, a rooftop pool and that familiar House ease.

items.name: ABaC Restaurant & Hotel
items.description: A small hotel above one of Spain's great restaurants, in the green calm of the upper city.

items.name: Nobu Hotel Barcelona
items.description: A tall, contemporary tower with a 23rd-floor pool and 360-degree views across the city.

items.name: Sofitel Barcelona Skipper
items.description: A French-run beach-side house opposite Hotel Arts, with rooftop pools over the Mediterranean.

items.name: W Barcelona
items.description: The sail-shaped tower at the end of the beach, the city's most photographed modern silhouette.

items.name: Hotel Neri, Relais & Châteaux
items.description: A 12th-century palace on a hidden Gothic-Quarter square, candlelit, intimate, deeply romantic.

items.name: Grand Hotel Central
items.description: A 1920s house between the Gothic Quarter and El Born, crowned by a rooftop infinity pool.

items.name: Kimpton Vividora Barcelona
items.description: A warm, art-filled house in the heart of the Gothic Quarter, with a rooftop bar and pool.

items.name: H10 Casa Mimosa
items.description: A quiet boutique with a garden terrace, a step from Gaudí's La Pedrera.

items.name: Yurbban Passage Hotel & Spa
items.description: A polished, well-run house on a passage near El Born, with a small rooftop pool.

items.name: Basílica de la Sagrada Família
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: Gaudí's unfinished masterpiece, the tallest church in the world since the Tower of Jesus Christ topped out at 172.5m in 2026. Go early or book a late slot to see the nave's stone-forest columns lit by the stained glass, warm reds and golds in the west windows at sunset, cool blues in the east at dawn. Buy timed tower access in advance; the lift up a spire is worth the vertigo.

items.name: Park Güell
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: Gaudí's whimsical hillside garden-city, all serpentine trencadís mosaic benches, the tiled salamander, and the terrace looking straight down to the sea. Book the timed Monumental Zone entry; arrive at opening to have the colonnaded viaducts to yourself before the crowds. The surrounding free park is a lovely, shaded stroll for families.

items.name: Casa Batlló
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: The most theatrical house on the block, a shimmering facade of broken blue-green glass, bone-like balconies, and a dragon's-back roof. The evening tours and the immersive light-and-sound installation on the top floor are the discreet way to see it without shoulder-to-shoulder crowds.

items.name: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: Gaudí's rippling stone apartment block, nicknamed 'the quarry.' The real prize is the rooftop, where the chimneys stand like helmeted warriors framing the Sagrada Família. Come back after dark for 'La Pedrera Night Experience,' a rooftop show with projections, an atmospheric, low-crowd evening.

items.name: Palau de la Música Catalana
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Palau de la Música Catalana and Hospital de Sant Pau
items.description: A modernista concert hall of stained glass, mosaic pillars and an inverted glass-dome skylight that floods the auditorium with daylight, Domènech i Montaner at his most exuberant. Take the guided tour, but far better: book a concert (the guitar recitals are magical) to hear it as it was meant to be experienced.

items.name: Recinte Modernista de Sant Pau (Hospital de Sant Pau)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Palau de la Música Catalana and Hospital de Sant Pau
items.description: The world's largest art nouveau site, a garden campus of mosaic-domed pavilions built as a hospital, now beautifully restored and refreshingly crowd-free. A short walk from the Sagrada Família and a serene counterpoint to it.

items.name: Museu Picasso
items.description: Set across five linked medieval palaces on Carrer Montcada, this holds the world's richest collection of Picasso's formative years, the classical training, the aching Blue Period, and his complete riff on Velázquez's 'Las Meninas.' Reserve ahead; the mansions themselves are half the pleasure.

items.name: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya (MNAC)
items.description: Housed in the palatial Palau Nacional above the Magic Fountain, MNAC holds the finest collection of Romanesque church frescoes on earth, murals lifted whole from remote Pyrenean chapels. The rooftop terrace has one of the best free-ish city panoramas.

items.name: Fundació Joan Miró
items.description: A luminous white building by Josep Lluís Sert, purpose-built to hold Miró's stars, symbols and sculptures with daylight and air. The sculpture roof-terrace and the calm hilltop setting make it the most restful of the big museums.

items.name: Barcelona Cathedral (La Seu)
items.description: The soaring Gothic cathedral of Santa Eulàlia, with a cloister where thirteen white geese are kept (one for each year of the child-martyr's life). Take the lift to the roof for a close view over the medieval rooftops. Dress modestly to enter.

items.name: Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar
items.description: The purest Catalan Gothic in the city, the 'cathedral of the sea,' raised in the 14th century by the port stevedores who hauled the stones themselves. The interior is austere and breathtaking; sit for the sublime acoustics or catch an evening concert.

items.name: Gothic Quarter (Barri Gòtic)
items.description: The medieval heart of Barcelona, a maze of narrow lanes, hidden plazas and Roman wall fragments. Wander without a map: find Plaça Sant Felip Neri with its shrapnel-scarred church, the Pont del Bisbe bridge, and cafés on Plaça Reial. Best early morning or late evening when the day-trippers thin out.

items.name: El Born neighbourhood
items.description: Barcelona's most stylish old quarter, designer boutiques, wine bars and craft ateliers threaded through medieval streets around Santa Maria del Mar. The Passeig del Born and Carrer Montcada are the spine; graze the tapas bars and independent shops at your own pace.

items.name: Gràcia neighbourhood
items.description: A former village that kept its own rhythm, leafy squares (Plaça del Sol, Plaça de la Vila) ringed by terrace cafés, independent designers and vermouth bars. The least touristy place to feel local Barcelona; time a visit to the wild Festa Major street-decoration festival in August.

items.name: La Rambla
items.description: The famous tree-lined promenade running from Plaça de Catalunya to the sea, flower stalls, the Boqueria market, and the mosaic by Miró underfoot at Pla de l'Os. Best walked briskly as a spine to the old town; keep valuables close, as it's pickpocket territory.

items.name: Mercat de la Boqueria
items.description: Barcelona's grand food cathedral, 300-plus stalls of jamón, seafood, fruit and jewel-bright juices under a modernista iron roof. Skip the entrance crush and go deep to the back where locals eat; the counter stools at Bar Pinotxo are an institution. Go before 10am for the calm, quality version.

items.name: Mercat de Santa Caterina
items.description: A working neighbourhood market under an undulating, candy-coloured mosaic roof by architect Enric Miralles. Far less touristed than the Boqueria, come for cheese, olives and a quiet counter lunch where locals actually shop.

items.name: Passeig de Gràcia
items.description: Barcelona's grandest avenue and its luxury-shopping spine, flagship maisons (Louis Vuitton, Chanel, Loewe) housed beneath the modernista facades of the 'Block of Discord,' where Casa Batlló and Casa Amatller sit side by side. The one address that rewards a discerning, unhurried afternoon.

items.name: Bunkers del Carmel (Turó de la Rovira)
items.description: A former Civil War anti-aircraft battery on a 262m hilltop with a full 360-degree sweep over the whole city to the sea. The locals' sunset spot, bring a bottle and a jacket. Free, but a proper climb; a taxi or private car to the base saves the legs.

items.name: Tibidabo & Sagrat Cor
items.description: Barcelona's highest point at 512m, crowned by the neo-Gothic Sagrat Cor church (take the lift to the roof) and a charming century-old amusement park with a Ferris wheel over the whole coastline. On a clear day you can see the Pyrenees. A great multi-generation half-day.

items.name: Montjuïc & the Cable Car (Telefèric)
items.description: The green hill above the port, laced with gardens, museums and Olympic venues. Ride the Telefèric de Montjuïc up to the 17th-century castle for harbour views, then wander down through the terraced gardens. A relaxed, uncrowded half-day away from the old-town bustle.

items.name: Magic Fountain of Montjuïc (Font Màgica)
items.description: A grand 1929 fountain that performs a free choreographed show of water, light and music below the illuminated Palau Nacional. An easy, crowd-pleasing evening for families, check the seasonal schedule, as shows run only certain nights.

items.name: Parc de la Ciutadella
items.description: The city's oldest and greenest public park, built for the 1888 World's Fair, a monumental cascade fountain (young Gaudí had a hand in it), a rowing lake, and shaded lawns. The nearest thing to a picnic-and-slow-down morning in central Barcelona; the zoo and parliament sit within it.

items.name: Barceloneta beach & boardwalk
items.description: The city beach, a broad crescent of sand backed by seafood terraces and the long Passeig Marítim promenade. Walk it at golden hour, hire a paddleboard, or book a private day sail out of Port Vell. For a calmer swim, the northern beaches (Bogatell, Nova Icària) are cleaner and quieter.

items.name: Port Vell & the waterfront
items.description: The revamped old harbour, superyacht marina, the Rambla de Mar footbridge, and the aquarium's shark tunnel for younger travellers. A pleasant stroll linking the Gothic Quarter to the beach; the marina is where private charters and sunset cruises depart.

items.name: Palau Güell
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: Gaudí's early, darker masterpiece, a six-storey city palace for his patron Eusebi Güell, built around a soaring parabolic-domed central hall pierced with starlight-like holes, and a roof of technicolour trencadís chimneys. Quiet and often overlooked, just off La Rambla.

items.name: Casa Vicens
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: Gaudí's very first house, a riot of green-and-white tiles, ironwork and Moorish motifs that shows the young genius already breaking every rule. Recently opened to the public and rarely crowded, the connoisseur's Gaudí stop.

items.name: Colònia Güell & Gaudí's Crypt
items.area: Santa Coloma de Cervelló (edge of Barcelona)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Works of Antoni Gaudí
items.description: A short train ride out of the city to Gaudí's astonishing brick-and-basalt crypt, the structural laboratory where he tested the leaning columns and catenary arches later used in the Sagrada Família. Set in a preserved modernista workers' village; peaceful and uncrowded.

items.name: Gran Teatre del Liceu
items.description: Barcelona's opera house since 1847 and one of the world's great lyric theatres, its gilded horseshoe auditorium rebuilt after a 1994 fire. Book a box for an opera or a recital, or take the guided tour of the mirror hall, the grand cultural evening in the city.

items.name: MACBA (Museu d'Art Contemporani de Barcelona)
items.description: Richard Meier's luminous white building anchoring gritty-cool El Raval, with a strong post-war and contemporary collection. The sloping plaza out front is Europe's most famous skateboarding spot, a bit of living street culture that pairs with the art inside.

items.name: CCCB (Centre de Cultura Contemporània)
items.description: The city's sharpest ideas venue, ambitious exhibitions on cities, technology and culture, film seasons and talks, set in a restored former almshouse next to MACBA. Where thoughtful travellers go to take Barcelona's intellectual pulse.

items.name: El Raval neighbourhood
items.description: Barcelona's most multicultural and fast-changing quarter, vintage shops on Carrer de la Riera Baixa, Rodríguez's fat cat sculpture on the Rambla del Raval, and a wave of new galleries and design bars. Edgy and characterful; wander in daylight and stay on the busier streets at night.

items.name: Poblenou & the beach neighbourhoods
items.description: A former industrial district reborn as Barcelona's creative-tech quarter, the leafy Rambla del Poblenou, converted-factory galleries, and quieter beaches (Bogatell) just beyond. Monthly design and vintage markets; a low-key, local counterpoint to the old town.

items.name: Poble Sec & Carrer de Blai
items.description: A neighbourhood at the foot of Montjuïc built around a pedestrian pintxo strip, bar after bar of Basque-style skewers at a euro or two apiece, plus Albert Adrià's acclaimed Bodega 1900 nearby. The relaxed, delicious local answer to a big dinner out.

items.name: Els Encants Vells (Fira de Bellcaire)
items.description: One of Europe's oldest flea markets, reborn under a spectacular mirrored-canopy roof, 300-plus stalls of antiques, vintage, curios and genuine treasure among the junk. Come with time and patience; the mornings (Mon/Wed/Fri/Sat) are best.

items.name: Mercat de Sant Antoni
items.description: A beautifully restored 19th-century iron market hall, everyday food shopping mid-week, and a beloved Sunday book, comic and collectors' market spilling around the outside. The surrounding streets have become one of the city's best low-key food-and-drink zones.

items.name: CosmoCaixa (Science Museum)
items.description: One of Europe's finest science museums, best known for its 'Flooded Forest', a full glasshouse slice of Amazon rainforest with live piranhas and crocodiles, and a towering geological wall of real rock. Superb, hands-on, and genuinely engaging for children and adults alike.

items.name: Parc del Laberint d'Horta
items.description: Barcelona's oldest garden (1791), a neoclassical estate with a romantic hedge maze, cypress avenues, pavilions and a still lake, capped at 750 visitors at a time so it stays serene. A hidden, aristocratic retreat far from the tourist trail; magical with children.

items.name: Poble Espanyol
items.description: An open-air 'Spanish village' of 117 buildings replicating architecture from every region, built for the 1929 Expo, plus artisan workshops, galleries and glassblowers at work. Touristy but genuinely fun for families; a painless way to sample all of Spain in an afternoon.

items.name: Spotify Camp Nou
items.description: FC Barcelona's colossal stadium, one of Europe's largest, freshly rebuilt and reopened. The immersive museum-and-pitch tour is a pilgrimage for football-mad families; match tickets, when the season's on, are the electric option.

items.name: Flamenco at Palau Dalmases
items.description: An intimate flamenco tablao inside a candlelit Baroque palace on Carrer Montcada, a single guitarist, singer and dancer at close range rather than a big touristy revue. The atmospheric way to experience the art form; book the early evening seating.

items.name: Bunker-to-beach vermouth & tapas crawl
items.description: The most Barcelona thing you can do, a slow graze between neighbourhood bars over vermut, pa amb tomàquet and small plates. A private food guide can tailor a route for vegetarian and Jain-friendly palates (escalivada, patatas, pan-con-tomate, market fruit) and skip the pork-heavy stops.

items.name: Montserrat monastery & mountain
items.description: A Benedictine monastery dramatically wedged into a jagged, saw-toothed massif, home to the revered 'Black Madonna' (La Moreneta) and the Escolania boys' choir, which sings most days. Ride the rack railway or cable car up, then walk the ridge trails. A private car and guide make it an effortless half-day of nature and pilgrimage.

items.name: Girona
items.area: Day trip (~40 min by high-speed train)
items.description: A jewel-box medieval city, a magnificent Gothic cathedral with the widest nave in the world, one of Europe's best-preserved Jewish quarters (El Call), and the pastel houses of the Onyar river (a 'Game of Thrones' backdrop). Nearby El Celler de Can Roca is one of the world's top restaurants; book far ahead.

items.name: Sitges
items.description: An elegant seaside town of white villas, modernista mansions and golden beaches, long a bohemian and artists' haunt. Stroll the promenade to the church on its headland, lunch on the seafront, and dip in the Mediterranean. The easy, glamorous coastal escape from the city.

items.name: Disfrutar
credentials: World's 50 Best Restaurants, No. 1 (2024), now in the Best of the Best hall of fame
items.description: The best restaurant in the world, three ex-elBulli chefs at the absolute summit of playful, avant-garde cooking.

items.name: Lasarte
items.description: Martín Berasategui and Paolo Casagrande's flawless haute cuisine, the first restaurant in Barcelona to hold three stars.

items.name: ABaC
items.description: Jordi Cruz's ambitious, half-classic half-avant-garde tasting menu, in the green calm of the upper city.

items.name: Cocina Hermanos Torres
items.description: The Torres twins cook in the middle of a vast open kitchen, theatre and three stars in an old tyre workshop.

items.name: Enigma
credentials: World's 50 Best Restaurants No. 34 (2025, new entry), only Catalan restaurant in the top 50
items.description: Albert Adrià's most personal project, a shifting, dreamlike journey through a series of rooms.

items.name: Enoteca Paco Pérez
items.description: Paco Pérez's sea-and-garden cooking on the seafront, two stars held for well over a decade.

items.name: Cinc Sentits
items.description: A deeply personal ode to Catalan produce and memory, raised to two stars and richly deserving.

items.name: Aleia
items.description: Ingredient-driven cooking inside Domènech i Montaner's Casa Fuster, gastronomy and architecture in one room.

items.name: Moments
items.description: The Ruscalleda family's refined Catalan cooking, in the calm of the Mandarin Oriental.

items.name: Mont Bar
items.description: Tapas raised to two-star technique, the most exciting small-plates room in the city.

items.name: Angle
items.description: Jordi Cruz's more accessible room, precise, contemporary Catalan cooking without the ABaC ceremony.

items.name: Dos Palillos
items.description: Albert Raurich's Asian-Spanish tapas at a black-lacquered counter, elBulli technique, izakaya soul.

items.name: Koy Shunka
items.description: Hideki Matsuhisa's Japanese counter in the Gothic Quarter, Barcelona's benchmark for sushi and kaiseki.

items.name: Caelis
items.description: Romain Fornell's classical French-Catalan cooking, and an intimate kitchen table for the curious.

items.name: Via Veneto
items.description: A Belle Époque institution open since 1967, grand, classical Catalan dining and a legendary cellar.

items.name: Oria
items.description: Martín Berasategui's Basque-rooted brasserie downstairs from Lasarte, refined, and a little easier to book.

items.name: Hofmann
items.description: The much-loved cooking school's restaurant, technically immaculate Mediterranean, and famous pastries.

items.name: Hisop
items.description: An intimate room doing quietly inventive, market-led Catalan cooking, a long-held, understated star.

items.name: Alkimia
items.description: Jordi Vilà's temple of modern Catalan cooking, inside a Moritz brewery, tradition, reimagined.

items.name: Xerta
items.description: The cooking of the Ebro delta brought to the city, rice, eel and river produce, done with real finesse.

items.name: Come by Paco Méndez
items.description: The successor to Hoja Santa, Paco Méndez's dazzling, avant-garde Mexican cooking.

items.name: Slow & Low
items.description: A young, personal kitchen weaving Catalan and Mexican threads, one of the city's most characterful stars.

items.name: Atempo
items.description: Jordi Cruz's third city star, refined, contemporary cooking in an elegant Eixample room.

items.name: Fishølogy
items.description: A bold newcomer built around 'charcuterie of the sea', one of the freshest ideas in the city.

items.name: MAE Barcelona
items.description: Inventive, globally-inspired cooking that earned a first star in the elegant upper city.

items.name: Prodigi
items.description: A precise, quietly ambitious newcomer, a first star for a kitchen worth seeking out.

items.name: Berbena
items.description: A tiny, characterful room doing seasonal Mediterranean plates with Asian and South-American touches.

items.name: Cruix
items.description: Chef Miquel Pardo's generous tasting menu, Castellón roots, brilliant value, always full.

items.name: Bacaro
items.description: A cramped, joyful Venetian kitchen hidden behind the Boqueria, cicchetti and fresh pasta done properly.

items.name: Vivanda
items.description: Catalan 'platillos' and monthly specials in a village-quiet corner of Sarrià, with a lovely terrace.

items.name: Avenir
items.description: An easy, well-priced neighbourhood room doing careful market cooking, a local favourite for good reason.

items.name: Saó BCN
items.description: Cooking built around 'ripeness', local produce, a French hand, and real value in the upper city.

items.name: Bardeni, el Meatbar
items.description: Dani Lechuga's meat-obsessed counter, steak tartare and cuts handled with real seriousness.

items.name: Glug
items.description: A young, spontaneous bistro with globally-inspired cooking and a wine list to match.

items.name: Oníric
items.description: A poetic, plant-forward kitchen, creative, seasonal cooking with vegetables at the centre.

items.name: Boadas
items.description: Barcelona's oldest cocktail bar, open since 1933, a tiny, standing-room Art Deco room where the drinks are shaken, not poured.

items.name: Banker's Bar, Mandarin Oriental
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel, a bar of real standing
items.description: The old bank vault of the Mandarin Oriental turned intimate cocktail bar, polished, discreet, and expertly made.

items.name: Sips
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 3), Best Bar in Europe
World's 50 Best Bars, No. 1 in the world (2023)
items.description: The best bar in the world in 2023, and Europe's best three years running, Simone Caporale and Marc Álvarez's cutting-edge cocktail counter.

items.name: Paradiso
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, No. 1 in the world (2022)
items.description: A speakeasy behind the fridge door of a pastrami shop, a whale-ribbed room and some of the most theatrical drinks anywhere.

items.name: Dr. Stravinsky
items.description: An apothecary of a bar, ferments, distillates and house ingredients lining the walls, from the Paradiso team.

items.name: Foco
items.description: A confident new arrival on the world list, inventive, produce-led drinks in an easy, modern room.

items.name: Terrat, Mandarin Oriental
credentials: Atop a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel, a landmark rooftop
items.description: The Mandarin Oriental's rooftop terrace and dipping pool, a considered drink above Passeig de Gràcia.

items.name: Two Schmucks
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, former top-50 listee (2021–2023)
items.description: A self-styled 'five-star dive bar' on a Raval side street, irreverent, warm, and seriously good at cocktails.

plan.heading: 4 days in Barcelona, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private early-access visit to the Sagrada Familia before opening, then the towers if you wish.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Park Guell in the late afternoon light, then a walk down through Gracia's squares.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Disfrutar, the world-ranked tasting room from the elBulli lineage.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Casa Batllo and La Pedrera on Passeig de Gracia, then the boutiques of the block.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Gothic Quarter and the Cathedral, then a walk to the marina at Port Vell.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Aperitivo on the roof of Hotel Casa Fuster, then dinner at Lasarte, Barcelona's three-Michelin table from Martin Berasategui.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Joan Miro Foundation and the Montjuic gardens, with the city and harbour below.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Picasso Museum in El Born, then vermouth and tapas in the barrio's lanes.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Enigma, Albert Adria's theatrical room, or classic seafood at Botafumeiro.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to the Penedes for a private cellar tour and tasting at a family cava house.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch among the vineyards, or instead a day at the beach clubs of the Costa Brava.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last night of tapas along Carrer de Blai, then a nightcap at the Cotton House bar.

items.name: Eixample
items.description: Wide modernista boulevards and Gaudí facades, central and elegant.

items.name: Gràcia
items.description: Village squares and independent bars, for a local, low-key stay.

items.name: Born / Gothic Quarter
items.description: Medieval lanes and nightlife, atmospheric but busy.

events.name: La Mercè
events.note: The city's patron-saint festival, with human towers, fire runs and street concerts.

events.name: Primavera Sound
events.note: One of Europe's leading music festivals, drawing global acts to the seafront.

events.name: Sant Jordi
events.note: Catalonia's day of books and roses, the streets fill with stalls and readers.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in the Eixample near Passeig de Gracia for elegance and Gaudi at your door; book Sagrada Familia and Park Guell ahead with a guide, and stay quietly alert to pickpockets on La Rambla and the metro.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Barcelona El Prat (BCN), where a chauffeured car meets you airside and reaches the centre in about twenty-five minutes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The city rewards walking through the Gothic Quarter and Eixample; keep a private driver for Montjuic, day trips and evenings, and use taxis freely as they are plentiful and honest.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Fast, ubiquitous 5G; a Spain or EU eSIM is effortless and wifi is everywhere.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards and contactless are accepted nearly everywhere, small cash is handy for markets, and a euro or two or rounding up is ample as tipping is modest.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September-October are best: warm, dry, swimmable sea without the August peak. Avoid August, when much of the city half-closes for holidays and heat and cruise crowds peak; winters are mild but cooler for the beach.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India. Best is one-stop via Gulf hubs (Qatar via Doha, Emirates via Dubai, Etihad via Abu Dhabi) or European hubs (Lufthansa via Frankfurt, Swiss via Zurich) into Barcelona El Prat (~11-14h total). IndiGo offers a codeshare via Istanbul with Turkish. For business/first, Qatar Qsuite or Lufthansa/Swiss First give the strongest cabins; Al Mourjan lounge in Doha is a standout connection.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; routine EU standards. Safe, but Barcelona has Europe's most persistent pickpocketing, especially on La Rambla, the metro and around Sagrada Familia, so stay alert with bags and phones. Tap water is safe but often tastes of chlorine; most prefer bottled.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very good for vegetarians and among the easier Spanish cities for it; Jain is workable with briefing (garlic, and check for hidden ham/fish stock). Strong Indian scene, e.g. Surya and Tandoori Nights; also excellent dedicated vegetarian dining such as Teresa Carles.
